title: Thinking like a historian: sources and evidence

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: The past is everything that has already happened. History is what historians build when they investigate it. This topic shows you how: by asking questions of sources, making careful inferences, and checking who made a source, when and why.

sections.title: 1. The past and History are not the same thing

blocks.p: The past happened once and is gone. We cannot visit it. History is the account people construct afterwards by investigating what survives: objects, documents, pictures, buildings and memories.

That is why two historians can know the same facts and still disagree. They may ask different questions, give different evidence more weight, or explain it differently. An account of the past made later is called an interpretation.

Thinking like a historian means asking: What happened? How do we know? How sure can we be? Over this unit you build a Historian's Toolkit of ideas: evidence, chronology, enquiry, cause and consequence, perspective, ethics, significance, change and continuity, and argument.

evidence: The past = what happened. History = how we investigate and explain it.
An interpretation is a later account or explanation of the past.

sections.title: 2. Sources and evidence

blocks.p: A source is anything that gives us information about the past. Historians often sort sources into four kinds:

ul: Written: letters, diaries, newspapers, laws, official records.
Oral: memories passed on by speaking, such as an interview with a grandparent or traditions passed down through a community.
Physical: objects and buildings, like pottery, coins, tools or a fort.

blocks.p: A source only becomes evidence when a historian uses it to answer a question. The same photograph of Dubai Creek could be evidence about boats, about trade, or about what people wore, depending on the question.
There is no single "best" type of source. It depends on what the historian wants to find out. Oral history matters especially where few written records survive.

evidence: A source becomes evidence when it is used to answer a question.
The best type of source depends on the question being asked.

sections.title: 3. Inference and provenance

blocks.p: An inference is a conclusion you reach from evidence, rather than something the source states directly. Historians move step by step: SOURCE → QUESTION → EVIDENCE → INFERENCE. A useful sentence pattern is: "I can see… This suggests… Therefore I can infer…"

Provenance means who made a source, when, where and why. It shapes what a source can tell us. A foreign visitor describing Dubai in the mid-20th century might notice things locals took for granted but miss things only locals understood. An Emirati recalling childhood decades later remembers from the inside, but memory can change over time. An official record may be precise but only cover what officials cared about.

A biased source is not useless. It may be excellent evidence of what its maker believed or wanted others to believe. The question is always: reliable for what? Historians check one source against others. This is called corroboration.

evidence: I can see → this suggests → therefore I can infer.
Ask "reliable for what?", not just "reliable or unreliable?"

misconceptions.right: History is investigating the past and building an argument from evidence. Facts matter, but historians also ask how we know and how sure we can be.
A biased source can be very useful, for example as evidence of what someone believed. Always ask "useful for what?"

misconceptions.wrong: An inference is just repeating what the source says.
misconceptions.right: An inference goes beyond the words or picture: it is what the evidence suggests.

misconceptions.wrong: Older sources are always more reliable.
misconceptions.right: Age does not make a source reliable. Provenance and the question you are asking matter more.

sources.title: Wilfred Thesiger's photographs of the Trucial Coast
sources.origin: Taken by a British explorer; now held in museum collections (Pitt Rivers Museum, Oxford).
sources.purpose: A personal record of his travels in Arabia.
sources.usefulness: Shows everyday life before oil wealth. It is an outsider's view, so we must ask what he chose to photograph and what he left out.

sources.title: Al Fahidi Fort
sources.origin: Built in Dubai; today it houses part of the Dubai Museum.
sources.purpose: Defence of the settlement, and later a ruler's residence and garrison.
sources.usefulness: Physical evidence of how early Dubai was defended and built. It does not tell us what ordinary people thought.

sources.title: Oral history interview with an Emirati elder
sources.date: Recorded recently about childhood decades ago
sources.origin: A person remembering their own experience.
sources.purpose: To preserve memories of life before rapid development.
sources.usefulness: Gives an insider's experience that official records miss. Memory can change over time, so historians corroborate it.

evidence.q: Explain how the provenance of a foreign visitor's description of mid-20th-century Dubai affects what it can tell a historian.
evidence.model: As an outsider, the visitor may notice things locals took for granted, such as daily routines, but may misunderstand or miss things only locals knew. So it is useful for how Dubai looked to outsiders, but historians should corroborate it.

evidence.q: Use the "I can see… This suggests… Therefore…" steps to make an inference from a photograph of wooden boats (dhows) crowded on Dubai Creek.
evidence.model: I can see many wooden dhows tied up close together on the creek. This suggests the creek was busy with trade or fishing. Therefore I can infer the sea was central to how people earned a living.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: Study a photograph of Dubai Creek from the late 1940s, showing wooden dhows and people unloading goods. What can you infer about life in Dubai at that time? Give two inferences, each supported with evidence from the source.
questions.asks: Make two inferences: things the photograph suggests but does not state. Back each one with a detail you can see.
steps: Look closely and list three things you can SEE.
For each, ask: what does this SUGGEST about life then?
Write two inferences using "I can see… This suggests… Therefore…".
questions.plan: 2 minutes looking and noting details, 5 minutes writing, 1 minute checking each inference has evidence.
success: Each backed by a precise detail from the source
Goes beyond describing what is shown
mistakes: Only describing the picture ("there are boats")

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "A biased source is useless to historians." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Decide how far you agree, using examples of sources and the idea of "reliable for what?". You must reach a judgement.
steps: Decide your view and how strongly (qualifier).
Give one example where bias limits a source.
Give one example where a biased source is still very useful.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning a point for each side, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking qualifiers and connectives.
success: Explains using "because / this meant that / therefore"
mistakes: Saying all biased sources are useless

model.t: I largely disagree that a biased source is useless, because its bias can itself be evidence.
For example, an official record written to celebrate a ruler might exaggerate his successes.
This means it is weak evidence of what really happened, but strong evidence of how the ruler wanted to be seen.
Therefore a biased source is useful; historians just need to ask "reliable for what?" and corroborate it.

full: P: I agree / disagree to a large / some extent that…
E: For example, a source such as… shows…
some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …

stretch.task: Can two historians know exactly the same facts and still disagree? Explain using an example.
Could bias actually make a source more useful for some questions? Give a precise example.
Before reading a source, predict from its provenance alone what it will notice and what it will miss. Then check your prediction.
Whose voices are hardest to find in sources about the past? Why might that be, and what can historians do about it?
